title: Volatility across expiries
objectives: Plot the term structure of implied volatility.
Compute forward vols from total variance and spot a calendar arbitrage.

screens.title: Vol by expiry
screens.prose: Each dot is the at-the-money vol of one expiry of `make_chain()`: its smile read at $m = 0$, the forward. Black-Scholes would give one flat line.
screens.question: How many vol points above the one-month vol is the one-year vol?

hints.text: Read the first and last dots.
One month: 0.1850. One year: 0.2196.

feedback.correct: The one-year vol is 3.46 points higher: the curve slopes up.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the one-month vol from the one-year vol, in percentage points.

byKey.frac: 0.0346 is the gap as a fraction. In vol points it is 3.46.
byKey.neg: That is the one-month vol less the one-year. The one-year dot is higher.

explain.text: The vol rises from 18.50% at one month to 21.96% at one year. This curve is the **term structure** of implied vol. Upward sloping is normal in calm markets; in a crisis short-dated vol spikes and it inverts.

screens.title: Variance adds up
screens.prose: The curve is **total implied variance** $w = \sigma^2 T$ at the money, for the planted surface. Drag the two dots along it. The caption reads the square root of the chord's slope.

derive.caption: $T_1$ = {{round(P1.x*12)}} months, $T_2$ = {{round(P2.x*12)}} months: chord vol {{P2.x > P1.x + 0.01 ? fixed(sqrt(max(P2.y - P1.y, 0)/(P2.x - P1.x)), 4) : "undefined"}}

screens.question: Put the dots at six months and one year. What does the caption show?

hints.text: Drag $T_1$ to 0.5 and $T_2$ to 1.0, then read the caption.

feedback.correct: Between six months and a year the chord gives 22.51% vol.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Place the dots at 0.5 and 1.0 and read the chord vol.

byKey.avg: That is the average of the two vols, 21.15% and 21.84%. The chord uses variances.
byKey.one: That is the one-year vol itself. The caption gives the vol between the two dates.

explain.text: From six months to a year, $w$ rises from 0.02237 to 0.04770. The rise over 0.5 years is a variance of 0.0507 per year, a vol of 22.51%. It is higher than both expiries' own vols, because the curve steepens.

screens.title: The forward vol
screens.prose: The chord's vol is the **forward vol** $\sigma_{1,2}$: the vol the market implies between $T_1$ and $T_2$. Derive it. Returns over $[0, T_1]$ and $[T_1, T_2]$ are uncorrelated, so their variances add.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: Variance to $T_2$ = variance to $T_1$ + variance from $T_1$ to $T_2$ (uncorrelated returns)
$\sigma_2^2 T_2 = \sigma_1^2 T_1 + \sigma_{1,2}^2 (T_2 - T_1)$ (each variance is vol squared times time)
$\sigma_{1,2}^2 = \dfrac{\sigma_2^2 T_2 - \sigma_1^2 T_1}{T_2 - T_1}$ (subtract $\sigma_1^2 T_1$, divide by $T_2 - T_1$)
$\sigma_{1,2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{w_2 - w_1}{T_2 - T_1}}$, real only if $w_2 \ge w_1$ (square root)

hints.text: Start from the statement about variances, before any symbols.
Each variance is $\sigma^2$ times its length of time.
Then solve for $\sigma_{1,2}^2$ and take the root last.

feedback.correct: Variances add, so the forward variance is the slope of $w$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Go from words, to an equation, to $\sigma_{1,2}^2$, to its root.

byKey.s4: The square root needs $\sigma_{1,2}^2$ first. It is the last line.

explain.text: Vols do not add across time; variances do. So the forward variance is the slope of total variance between the two expiries. The root exists only when $w$ does not fall, which is the calendar no-arbitrage condition.

screens.title: Forward vols from the chain
screens.prose: The steps are the forward vols between consecutive expiries of the chain, drawn month by month. The dots are the at-the-money vols they come from.
screens.question: From $\sigma_1 = 0.2123$ at six months and $\sigma_2 = 0.2196$ at one year, what is the forward vol?

hints.text: Work out the two total variances.

feedback.correct: The market implies 22.67% vol for the second half-year.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the total variances, divide by 0.5, then take the root.

byKey.avg: You averaged the two vols. Vols do not add over time; use the total variances.
byKey.nosqrt: That is the forward variance. Take its square root to get a vol.

explain.text: $\sqrt{(0.04822 - 0.02254)/0.5} = 0.2267$, against the planted surface's 0.2251. Every forward vol sits above the spot vol before it, because the term structure rises. The small gaps are quote noise in the at-the-money reads.

screens.title: An inverted curve
screens.prose: In a sell-off short-dated vol spikes. A hand term structure: 45% at one month, 35% at three months and 28% at one year. Total variances: 0.016875, 0.030625 and 0.0784.
screens.question: What is the forward vol from one month to three months?

hints.text: The gap in time is two months, $2/12$ of a year.

feedback.correct: 28.72%: the market expects the storm to calm.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the rise in total variance by two months, then take the root.

byKey.avg: You averaged 45% and 35%. The forward vol uses variances, and it is lower than both.
byKey.nosqrt: That is the forward variance per year. Its root is the vol.

explain.text: When the curve inverts, forward vols fall below the spot vols: 28.7% from one to three months, 25.2% from three months to a year. Total variance still rises, so there is no arbitrage. It just rises more slowly.

screens.title: Variance that falls
screens.prose: A stale screen shows the one-month option at 40% and the two-month at 26%. Total variance: $0.40^2/12 = 0.01333$ and $0.26^2 \times 2/12 = 0.01127$.
screens.question: What does the forward vol between the two expiries say?

options.text: It is undefined: total variance falls, which is a calendar arbitrage

options.why: You took the root of a negative number by dropping its sign. A vol cannot be negative; the quotes are inconsistent.

options.text: It is low, about 12%: the market expects calm
options.why: The forward variance is $(0.01127 - 0.01333) \cdot 12 < 0$. There is no real vol, low or high.

options.text: Nothing: vols may fall with expiry
options.why: Vols may fall, as in the sell-off. Total variance may not.

hints.text: Is $w_2 - w_1$ positive?
A negative forward variance has no real square root.

feedback.correct: Falling total variance cannot be a real market.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the sign of $w_2 - w_1$ before taking any root.

byKey.neg: A negative variance has no vol at all. It is a sign the prices are wrong or stale.

explain.text: Sell the one-month option and buy the two-month one at the same strike: you receive more than you pay for less total variance. At the first expiry you are still holding the longer option, worth at least the short one. `forward_vol` raises `ValueError` here.

screens.title: Averaging vols
screens.prose: One month at 40% vol (results are due) and one year at 20%. A colleague wants the vol for the eleven months after the first.
screens.question: What is the forward vol from one month to one year?

options.why: You subtracted vol times time, $(0.2 - 0.4/12)/(11/12)$. Vols do not add over time; variances do.
You assumed the one-year vol holds throughout. The first month used up more than its share of the variance.
You averaged 40% and 20%. That ignores how long each vol applies.

hints.text: Work in total variance: $w_1 = 0.4^2/12$, $w_2 = 0.2^2$.

feedback.correct: 17.1%: after the results, the market expects a quiet year.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract total variances, not vols.

byKey.voladd: You treated vol as additive in time. Square the vols first: variance is what adds.

explain.text: $(0.04 - 0.01333)/(11/12) = 0.02909$, a vol of 17.1%. The vol-additive answer, 18.2%, overstates it by a point. Interpolating vols linearly makes the same error between expiries.

screens.title: The term structure in code
screens.prose: The dashboard's term-structure panel. For each expiry, take `smile(...)`, drop NaN vols, sort by $m$, and interpolate linearly at $m = 0$, the forward. Return a Series indexed by expiry, named `atm_iv`.
screens.question: Complete `atm_term_structure(clean, S, r, q)`.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests: a hand chain with a known term structure and the seeded chain, to 4 places. The first run loads numpy and pandas, about 15 seconds.

hints.text: `np.interp(0.0, xs, ys)` needs `xs` in rising order.
`sm.dropna(subset=["iv"]).sort_values("m")`.
`out[float(T)] = float(np.interp(0.0, sm["m"], sm["iv"]))`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the sort by $m$ and that NaN vols are dropped first.

explain.text: Interpolating at $m = 0$ reads the smile at the forward. At three months it sits between the 100 put ($m = -0.02$) and the 105 call. Past the last quote, `np.interp` holds the end value flat, so a lopsided expiry still gets a number; the note should say so.

screens.prose: Now the forward vol. Raise `ValueError` when $T_2 \le T_1$, and when total variance falls. Equal total variances give a forward vol of exactly 0.

Check its sign before the root.
`if fwd_var < 0: raise ValueError(...)`, then `return sqrt(fwd_var)`.

screens.title: Pricing an earnings day
screens.prose: A share reports results in 22 days. The 20-day option trades at 24% vol; the 27-day option, which spans the results, at 34%. Assume the share's ordinary vol is 24% on every day.
screens.question: What one-day move, as a standard deviation, does the market price for the results?

hints.text: At 24% for all 27 days the variance would be $0.24^2 \times 27/365$.
The extra variance is $(0.34^2 - 0.24^2) \times 27/365 = 0.00429$.
Its square root is the results-day move: 6.55%.

feedback.correct: About a 6.55% move, one standard deviation, on results day.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the variance the 27-day option carries beyond 24% vol, then take its root.

byKey.volpts: 10 vol points is the gap in annual vols. Convert to variance over 27 days first.
byKey.allvar: That is the root of the whole 27-day variance. Take away the ordinary days' share first.

explain.text: Total variance jumps by 0.00429 across the results, a 6.55% one-day move. Traders compare this with past results-day moves to decide whether event vol is cheap. It is a forward variance, concentrated on one date.

ideas: The term structure is at-the-money vol, read at the forward, against expiry: 18.5% at one month rising to 22.0% at one year in the seeded chain.
Variances add over time, not vols. Total variance $w = \sigma^2 T$ must not fall with expiry; its slope is the forward variance.
Forward vols price the market's view of each future period, such as an earnings day. A falling $w$ means stale or arbitrageable quotes.

formula.name: Forward vol
formula.note: Defined only when $\sigma_2^2 T_2 \ge \sigma_1^2 T_1$; otherwise the quotes allow a calendar arbitrage.

summary.trap: Averaging or subtracting vols across expiries: from 40% at one month and 20% at a year the forward vol is 17.1%, not 18.2% or 30%.
